variants.name: CompletableFuture / CompletionStage continuations
variants.implementation_notes: Java has no language-level async construct, so the ACT is a java.base object: a CompletableFuture is both the token the caller holds and the producer side (complete/completeExceptionally), and continuations registered with whenComplete/handle capture the completion action and its state, so the completion is demultiplexed through the stage graph instead of by looking the request up. The registry (Map<requestId, CompletableFuture>) is only needed when the completing side cannot reach the stage object. Java 21's virtual threads and structured concurrency remove the need for a token wherever blocking thread-per-task code is affordable - prefer them there.
pitfalls: The thread that completes a stage may run the continuation: a blocking whenComplete handler stalls the I/O thread, and *Async overloads without an executor use the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
Exception precedence must be deliberate: a whenComplete action that throws completes the returned stage exceptionally, so 'log and continue' handlers silently change the pipeline.
Stages kept in a registry but never removed (timeout, cancellation) retain their continuations and captured state.

variants.name: SelectionKey attachment (NIO registration token)
variants.implementation_notes: NIO carries the pattern's name almost literally: attach(handler) stores one arbitrary object per channel registration and attachment() returns it when the selector reports readiness, so the key is the token and the attachment is the completion state - a reactor demultiplexes thousands of registrations without any request-id lookup. The object is single-valued, so a registration that needs several pieces of state must package them into one holder.
pitfalls: attach() replaces the previous attachment and returns it; code that re-attaches without saving/restoring silently loses the old operation's state.
Cancelled keys are only removed during the next selection operation, so an attachment can outlive the logical operation unless it is explicitly nulled out.

variants.name: ExecutorCompletionService completion queue
variants.implementation_notes: Queued completion notifications in the JDK: submit tasks to an ExecutorCompletionService and pull finished Futures from its completion queue - the Future (carrying the task handle) is the returned token, and the client decides when to consume completions instead of being called back. Suits batch fan-out and servers that pace their own scheduling; a bounded completion queue can make the completion wrapper's Queue.add fail, leaving that task's Future unretrievable, so use an unbounded queue or an explicit loss/backpressure policy.
pitfalls: Wrong move: supply a bounded completion queue without handling enqueue failure -> the completion wrapper's Queue.add can fail and the finished Future becomes unretrievable -> instead use an unbounded queue or define and monitor an explicit overflow policy.
The map keyed on the returned Future is the registry - entries not removed after take() leak request state.
